lead: Bulk forming squeezes a solid metal billet into a new shape without cutting away chips. This unit covers the four shop-floor processes that do it — rolling, forging, extrusion, and wire and tube drawing — the yield ideas that predict when the metal will flow, and powder metallurgy, where loose powder is pressed and heated into a part. After it you can choose a process for a shape, estimate the force it needs, and name the defect that appears when friction or force is wrong.
about: The unit moves from the metal itself to the machine that shapes it. Chapter 2.1 gives the flow curve, the two yield criteria (Tresca and von Mises) and the hot–cold working split; every later force calculation starts from that flow stress. Chapters 2.2 to 2.5 take the four bulk processes one by one — rolling, forging, extrusion, wire and tube drawing — each with its principle, equipment, defects and typical products. Chapter 2.6 collects the load and power formulas for all of them in one place. Chapter 2.7 then changes track to powder metallurgy, where the shape comes from compaction and sintering instead of a squeeze in a die.

chapters.idea: Metal flows permanently once its stress passes a yield limit, and that limit rises with strain in cold working but stays flat in hot working.
chapters.depth: True stress and true strain against engineering values, flow curve σ = Kεⁿ with K the strength coefficient and n the strain-hardening exponent, mean flow stress σ̄ = Kεⁿ/(n+1). Yield criteria: Tresca (maximum shear stress, σ₁ − σ₃ = σy) and von Mises (distortion energy, σy = √(σ₁² + σ₂² − σ₁σ₂) in plane stress), and the plane-strain yield value 1.15σy. Compare hot and cold working: temperature, force, surface finish, tolerance, strain hardening, recrystallisation. Recrystallisation temperature ≈ 0.4 Tm on the Kelvin scale; mention warm working in one line. Some syllabi call this section plasticity or yield theories. Depth: enough to compute flow stress and decide hot or cold.

figure.aria: A plot of flow stress against true strain: the cold-working curve rises steeply and flattens, while the hot-working line stays flat at about 120 MPa.

chapters.example: A mild steel bar is cold worked to a true strain of 0.15. Its flow curve is σ = 550 ε^0.25 MPa. Find the flow stress at the end of the pass, the mean flow stress, and the recrystallisation temperature (melting point 1500 °C). Answer: 0.15^0.25 = 0.622, so σ = 550 × 0.622 = 342 MPa; σ̄ = 342/(0.25 + 1) = 274 MPa; recrystallisation temperature = 0.4 × 1773 K = 709 K ≈ 436 °C, so working at 900 °C is hot working.
chapters.trap: Using engineering stress and strain, which fall after the ultimate point, instead of true values that keep rising. Also quoting one yield criterion as if Tresca and von Mises agree — they differ by about 15%, and plain strain yields at 1.15σy, not σy.
chapters.prereq: None inside the unit; needs the basic stress–strain curve from engineering mechanics.
chapters.leave: Recrystallisation and grain growth theory to a materials course; friction and die pressure to 2.6.

chapters.idea: Two rotating rolls pull a strip through a gap narrower than its thickness, so the strip gets thinner and longer.
chapters.depth: Principle, the roll-bite condition μ ≥ tan α and the maximum draft Δh_max = μ²R with R the roll radius, contact length L = √(RΔh), neutral point, forward and backward slip. Mills: two-high, three-high, four-high, cluster (Sendzimir), tandem, reversing roughing. Hot rolling from slab to coil, cold rolling with annealing and better finish, roll camber and roll bending for crown control. Defects: wavy edges, edge cracking, centre buckle, alligatoring, laps and seams, scale, roll marks. Products: bloom, billet, slab, plate, sheet, strip, rail. Some syllabi say flat rolling and shape rolling.

figure.title: Hot strip mill line
figure.aria: A flow chart of a hot strip mill: reheat furnace, reversing roughing mill, finishing train, run-out cooling table and down coiler.

chapters.example: A 250 mm wide strip is rolled from 20 mm to 15 mm in one pass on rolls of radius 300 mm, with friction coefficient 0.10. Is the pass possible? Find the contact length. Draft = 20 − 15 = 5 mm. Maximum draft = μ²R = 0.01 × 300 = 3 mm, which is less than 5 mm, so the pass fails. It needs μ ≥ √(5/300) = 0.13, or two passes. Contact length L = √(300 × 5) = 38.7 mm.
chapters.trap: Putting the roll diameter into Δh_max = μ²R instead of the radius, and confusing draft (mm) with reduction ratio (no unit). Also forgetting that a heavier draft needs more friction, not more force alone.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for flow stress and the hot–cold split.
chapters.leave: Roll pass design for rails and sections, and roll material selection, to a dedicated course.

chapters.idea: Repeated local squeezing between dies turns a billet into a shaped part whose grain flow follows the contour, so it is stronger than a machined part.
chapters.depth: Types: open-die (upsetting, drawing out, fullering, edging, swaging, punching), impression or closed-die (blocker and finisher impressions, flash, gutter), precision forging, upset forging and heading, roll forging, rotary swaging. Hammer, press and upsetter compared in one table. Full operation sequence for a connecting rod. Forging temperature ranges for steel, aluminium and copper alloys. Defects: unfilled section, cold shut (lap), flash crack, scale pit, die shift (mismatch), internal cracks, decarburisation, burnt metal. Grain flow, flash trimming, applications: crankshaft, connecting rod, railway wheel, spanner.

figure.title: Closed-die forging sequence
figure.aria: A step-by-step flow of closed-die forging: billet heating, upsetting, edging, blocking, finishing and trimming.

chapters.example: A cylindrical billet 80 mm diameter and 100 mm long is upset forged to a height of 60 mm. Find the final diameter and the average contact area. Volume constancy gives d₂ = d₁√(h₁/h₂) = 80 × √(100/60) = 103.3 mm. Volume = (π/4) × 80² × 100 = 502,650 mm³, so final area = 502,650/60 = 8,378 mm². If the mean flow stress is 250 MPa and the friction multiplier is 1.2, the press load is about 1.2 × 250 × 8,378 = 2.5 MN (load formulas in 2.6).
chapters.trap: Assuming closed-die forging needs no flash — the flash gap is what builds the die pressure that fills the cavity. Also mixing up cold shut (a folded lap) with unfilled section (metal that never reached the corner).
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for hot working and flow stress.
chapters.leave: Hammer and press construction to machine tools; post-forging heat treatment to a heat treatment course; forging defect inspection to the welding and joining unit.

chapters.idea: A ram pushes a billet through a die opening, so the metal takes the die cross-section as a continuous length.
chapters.depth: Direct (forward) extrusion: billet moves, friction on the whole container wall. Indirect (backward): die sits on a hollow ram, no billet–container friction. Impact extrusion: a punch hits a slug in a die, used for toothpaste tubes and battery cases. Hydrostatic extrusion in brief. Hot against cold extrusion, extrusion ratio R = A₀/A_f, die angle, dead-metal zone, tube extrusion over a mandrel and by port-hole die. Defects: pipe (tailpipe), surface cracking and bambooing, internal chevron cracking, die lines, blistering. Horizontal hydraulic press, typical products such as aluminium window sections and heat sinks.

figure.aria: A classification tree of extrusion into direct, indirect, impact and hydrostatic, each with a one-line note on how the ram or fluid acts.

chapters.example: A 100 mm diameter aluminium billet is direct extruded into a 40 mm diameter bar. Find the extrusion ratio, the ideal pressure and the ram force if the mean flow stress is 200 MPa. R = (100/40)² = 6.25. Ideal pressure p = σ̄ ln R = 200 × ln 6.25 = 200 × 1.833 = 367 MPa. Ram area = (π/4) × 100² = 7,854 mm², so F = 367 × 7,854 = 2.88 MN. Area reduction = 1 − 1/6.25 = 84%.
chapters.trap: Computing R as a diameter ratio instead of an area ratio, and saying indirect extrusion removes die friction — it removes billet–container friction, while die friction remains in both.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for hot and cold working and for mean flow stress.
chapters.leave: Impact-extrusion tooling detail to a tool design course; hydrostatic extrusion equipment to a special processes elective.

chapters.idea: A rod or wire is pulled, not pushed, through a converging die, and the pulling stress must stay below the metal's own yield strength or the wire breaks.
chapters.depth: Wire drawing: die zones (bell, approach angle, bearing or land, back relief), single-hole and multi-hole machines with capstan, bull block, drawing speed, lubrication, carbide and diamond dies, dry and wet drawing, patented and galvanised wire. Tube drawing: tube sinking with no internal support, fixed plug, floating plug, moving mandrel; effect on wall thickness. Defects: centre burst and chevron cracking in wire, die scratches and wear, breakage, eccentric bore and wall-thickness variation in tubes. Industrial area reduction per pass (about 20 %; the ideal limit is about 63 %).

figure.title: Two-pass wire drawing
figure.aria: A flow chart of two-pass wire drawing: rod, cleaning and coating, first die, capstan pull, anneal, second die.

chapters.example: A 5 mm wire is drawn to 4 mm in one pass. Mean flow stress is 350 MPa and the friction-and-shape factor is 1.3. Find the draw stress and check the pass is safe. ln(A₀/A_f) = ln(25/16) = 0.446, so σd = 1.3 × 350 × 0.446 = 203 MPa. The ratio σd/σ̄ = 203/350 = 0.58, below 1, so the wire survives the pass. Area reduction = 1 − 16/25 = 36 %.
chapters.trap: Using the push (extrusion) formula, or forgetting the safety check σd < σy. A pass whose draw stress exceeds the yield strength breaks the wire, however large the press.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for flow stress, 2.4 for the die-pressure idea shared with extrusion.
chapters.leave: Wire rope and cable making, and Mannesmann tube piercing, to product-specific notes.

chapters.idea: Every bulk forming load is a mean flow stress times a contact area, corrected for friction and shape.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it short. Roll force F = σ̄ w L with L = √(RΔh), torque per roll T = F L/2, power = 2Tω. Forging load F = σ̄ A K_f with K_f the friction-hill factor (about 1 + 2μr/3h for a disc). Extrusion pressure p = σ̄ (a + b ln R), ideal case a = 0, b = 1; drawing σd = σ̄ ln(A₀/A_f) × friction factor. Ideal work per unit volume, efficiency, press tonnage selection, energy per part — one line each.

figure.aria: A plot of extrusion pressure against extrusion ratio: both lines rise logarithmically, and the friction line sits above the ideal line by a constant factor.

chapters.example: A 300 mm wide strip is rolled from 10 mm to 7 mm on rolls of radius 250 mm. The mean flow stress is 350 MPa and the mill runs at 50 rev/min. Estimate the roll force and the power. L = √(250 × 3) = 27.4 mm. F = 350 × 27.4 × 300 = 2.88 × 10⁶ N ≈ 2.9 MN. Torque per roll = F L/2 = 2.88 × 10⁶ × 0.0137 = 39.4 kN·m. ω = 2π × 50/60 = 5.24 rad/s, so power = 2 × 39,400 × 5.24 = 413 kW.
chapters.trap: Treating a pressure in MPa as a force, forgetting the area multiplier, and using the billet area instead of the contact area under the rolls. Also mixing mm and m inside √(RΔh).
chapters.prereq: 2.1 to 2.5, since each formula reuses that chapter's geometry.
chapters.leave: The full slab-method derivation and finite element simulation to a plasticity course.

chapters.idea: Metal powder is pressed into a shape and heated below melting point so the particles weld together, giving a part with little or no machining.
chapters.depth: Powder making: water and gas atomisation, oxide reduction, electrolysis, pulverising, carbonyl process. Powder tests: particle size and shape, apparent density, tap density, flow rate. Blending and mixing, lubricants such as zinc stearate. Compaction: die pressing, cold and hot isostatic pressing, roll compaction, metal injection moulding in one line. Green density and green strength. Sintering: three stages, temperature 0.7 to 0.8 Tm, protective atmospheres (hydrogen, nitrogen, endogas), furnaces, spark discharge (spark plasma) sintering in brief. Finishing: sizing, coining, repressing, resintering, infiltration, impregnation. Properties: density, porosity, strength, ductility, hardness. Advantages, limitations, applications: gears, bushes, self-lubricating bearings, tungsten carbide inserts, magnets.

figure.title: Powder metallurgy route
figure.aria: A flow chart of the powder metallurgy route: atomising, blending, die compaction, sintering, sizing and inspection.

chapters.example: An iron gear blank of volume 12.5 cm³ is die compacted to a green density of 6.8 g/cm³; solid iron has density 7.87 g/cm³. Find the powder mass and the green porosity, and give a sintering temperature. Mass = 12.5 × 6.8 = 85 g. Porosity = 1 − 6.8/7.87 = 0.136, that is 13.6 %. Iron melts at 1538 °C (1811 K), so sintering is at 0.7–0.8 Tm ≈ 1270–1450 K, roughly 1000–1175 °C; a common value is 1120 °C in a hydrogen–nitrogen atmosphere.
chapters.trap: Saying sintering melts the powder — it stays solid and the particles bond by diffusion. Also using the solid density in place of the green density when computing mass, or mixing apparent density with green density.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for the plastic deformation of particles during compaction; the casting unit for the contrast with solidification.
chapters.leave: Metal injection moulding and binder jetting to the additive manufacturing unit; hot isostatic pressing and selective laser sintering to Unit 7.
